title: Emergence Delirium & Postoperative Delirium (PACU)

changelog.change: Initial entry — a genuine content gap (Content audit 2026-09-15, fresh-look Batch 8). CAM-ICU (ICU delirium) and Modified Aldrete (PACU discharge readiness) already existed, but nothing addressed recognition/management of emergence agitation or postoperative delirium specifically in the perioperative/PACU context.

summary: Emergence delirium (agitation in the minutes right after waking, classically a preschool-aged-child-plus-volatile-agent picture) and postoperative delirium (hours to days later, classically an elderly/ASA-high/prolonged-surgery picture) are related but distinct entities — know which one you're looking at, and always rule out a reversible physiologic cause first before assuming it's either.
whyThisMatters: These two entities are easy to lump together as 'the patient is confused after anesthesia,' but they have different risk populations, different time courses, and somewhat different management approaches — and both can mask a genuinely reversible physiologic problem (hypoxia, pain, a full bladder, residual paralysis) that gets missed if the agitation is reflexively attributed to 'just' emergence delirium or POD without a basic physiologic check first.
clinicalTakeaway: Emergence delirium: agitation/confusion in the minutes immediately after waking, classic risk pattern is preschool-aged children, volatile anesthetic maintenance, otolaryngology/ophthalmologic procedures, and preoperative anxiety — usually self-limited over minutes, but manage safely (prevent self-injury/line removal) and consider dexmedetomidine if prevention/treatment is needed. Postoperative delirium (POD): a fluctuating attention/awareness disturbance emerging hours to days after surgery, classic risk pattern is older age, higher ASA class, prolonged surgery/anesthesia time, greater blood loss, and low postoperative albumin — assess with a validated tool (CAM-ICU in the ICU setting) and address contributing factors (pain, sleep disruption, polypharmacy, sensory deprivation) as first-line management. Before attributing agitation/confusion to either entity, actively rule out a reversible physiologic cause: hypoxia, hypoglycemia, uncontrolled pain, a distended bladder, or residual neuromuscular blockade — these mimic or worsen both pictures and are fixable.

rows: Minutes — immediately upon emergence, in PACU
Preschool-aged children (though can occur in adults too)
Older adults, especially with higher ASA class
Volatile anesthetic maintenance, otolaryngology/ophthalmologic procedures, preoperative anxiety
Prolonged surgery/anesthesia time, greater intraoperative blood loss, low postoperative albumin, pre-existing cognitive impairment, polypharmacy
Usually self-limited, resolving over minutes as full alertness returns
Fluctuating course over hours to days; can persist and is associated with worse longer-term outcomes if unaddressed

body.text: Rule out a reversible cause FIRST — for either entity

Before attributing new agitation or confusion to 'just' emergence delirium or POD, actively check for and address a reversible physiologic cause — this is the single highest-value step and is easy to skip when the picture superficially fits the expected pattern.

items: Hypoxia — check oxygenation directly rather than assuming it's adequate.
Hypoglycemia — a quick point-of-care glucose check.
Uncontrolled pain — agitation can be the presenting sign of inadequately treated pain, particularly in a patient who can't yet verbally report it clearly.
A distended bladder — a common, easily overlooked contributor, especially after a procedure with intraoperative fluids and no interval voiding.

Residual neuromuscular blockade — an under-reversed or residually paralyzed patient can present with agitation/distress; confirm adequate reversal (see neuromuscular-blockade-reversal) rather than assuming full recovery.
Ensure patient safety first — prevent self-injury, line/tube removal, or falling, with appropriate physical safeguards/staffing rather than reflexive chemical restraint as the first move.

DEXMEDETOMIDINE is the most consistently evidence-supported pharmacologic option across both entities — intranasal dosing has been studied for pediatric emergence delirium prevention/treatment, and IV dosing is used in both pediatric and adult/elderly populations; it provides sedation without the respiratory depression of many alternatives and has shown benefit for reducing both emergence delirium incidence and postoperative delirium in various studied populations.

For POD specifically: assess with a validated screening tool (CAM-ICU in the ICU setting — see cam-icu) and address the broader contributing picture — adequate but not excessive analgesia, sleep-wake cycle preservation, early mobilization, minimizing deliriogenic medications, and correcting sensory deprivation (glasses/hearing aids back in place) — this multicomponent approach mirrors the broader PADIS/ICU delirium-prevention bundle already covered in padis-bundle.
For pediatric emergence delirium specifically: a calm, quiet recovery environment and parental presence at bedside (where institutional policy allows) can help alongside pharmacologic measures.
